questions.q: What is the first step in building a real executive dashboard, according to this lesson's process?
options: Answer the four audience questions from Lesson 62 for the actual executive audience
Choose the visual theme colors
Add every available metric to the canvas
Publish the report to the Power BI service
questions.explain: Every later decision — which metrics, where they go, how they're visualized — depends on first understanding who the dashboard is actually for.

questions.q: What must a KPI have before it earns a spot on the finished dashboard?
options: A target to compare against, not just a raw value, and it must pass the 'would this change a decision' test
It must be displayed using a pie chart
It must be the only metric on the page
It must be calculated using an iterator function
questions.explain: This directly reapplies Lesson 63's test — a metric without a target or without decision relevance doesn't belong as a headline KPI.

questions.q: What should be absent from a well-built executive dashboard, based on the finished example in this lesson?
options: 3D effects, excessive unrepeated colors, and charts competing for attention with each other
Any use of card visuals
Any charts sorted by category
More than one page in the report
questions.explain: The sample dashboard avoids exactly the distortions and inconsistencies covered in Lesson 65 — nothing fights for attention, and color/scale stay consistent throughout.

questions.q: What does the pre-launch checklist in this lesson ask you to verify?
options: That every tile traces back to an audience need, every KPI has a target, the most important number is seen first, and it fits one screen
That every visual type available in Power BI has been used at least once
That the dashboard has exactly ten tiles
That every chart uses a different color palette
questions.explain: The checklist is a final pass reapplying every principle from Lessons 62 through 65, not a new set of rules.

questions.q: What does this lesson say comes next, after a dashboard is well-designed?
options: It still needs to reach its audience — published, shared, and kept current, which Chapter 9 (Power BI Service & Fabric) covers
Nothing further is needed once the design is finished
The dashboard must be rebuilt entirely in the Power BI service
Chapter 9 covers building a second, alternate version of the same dashboard
questions.explain: Good design alone doesn't get a dashboard in front of its audience — workspaces, publishing, and access control are the next real hurdle, covered in Chapter 9.
